title: Which kings of Egypt were the Pharaohs of the oppression and the exodus?
summary: Exodus tells of a new king who knew not Joseph, of his death, and of the Pharaoh whom Moses faced, and names none of them. Later books name kings of Egypt. Which king oppressed Israel, and which let them go, is not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 1:8: “Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph.” Hebrew (WLC) 1:8: וַיָּ֥קָם מֶֽלֶךְ־חָדָ֖שׁ עַל־מִצְרָ֑יִם אֲשֶׁ֥ר לֹֽא־יָדַ֖ע אֶת־יֹוסֵֽף [and there arose a new king over Egypt who did not know Joseph]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:8: Ἀνέστη δὲ βασιλεὺς ἕτερος ἐπʼ Αἴγυπτον, ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει τὸν Ἰωσήφ [and there arose another king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph]. KJV 1:11: “And they built for Pharaoh treasure cities, Pithom and Raamses.” KJV 2:23: “And it came to pass in process of time, that the king of Egypt died”. KJV 5:1: “And afterward Moses and Aaron went in, and told Pharaoh, Thus saith the Lord God of Israel, Let my people go”. KJV 1 Kings 6:1: “in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel were come out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon”. KJV 1 Kings 11:40: “unto Shishak king of Egypt”. KJV 2 Kings 23:29: “Pharaohnechoh king of Egypt”. KJV Jeremiah 44:30: “Pharaohhophra king of Egypt”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO01.htm.
reasoning: The story turns on at least two kings: the one who began the oppression and died, and the one who refused Moses and then let Israel go. Each is called only “the king of Egypt” or “Pharaoh”. Who they were decides when the events are placed and against which Egyptian records they can be compared, so the gap is a material one. It is not that the books never name Egyptian kings: Shishak, Pharaohnechoh and Pharaohhophra are named in Kings and Jeremiah.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That the two kings can be identified from the city name Raamses at 1:11, or from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 counted back from Solomon, are both readings; they lead to different kings, and neither passage names one. This record asserts neither. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “Pharaoh” joined to a further name and for the words Shishak, So king, and Tirhakah; the verses found are in Kings, Chronicles, Isaiah and Jeremiah and concern later centuries. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G is proposed: at 1:8 Brenton’s Greek has “another king” where the KJV has “a new king”, a difference too slight to tag. No claim is made about Egyptian history. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: Who were “the priests” at Sinai, before Aaron and his sons were appointed?
summary: At Sinai the Lord speaks of “the priests, which come near to the Lord”. Aaron and his sons are not set apart for the priest’s office until chapter 28. Who these earlier priests of Israel were is not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 19:22: “And let the priests also, which come near to the Lord, sanctify themselves, lest the Lord break forth upon them.” Hebrew (WLC) 19:22: וְגַ֧ם הַכֹּהֲנִ֛ים הַנִּגָּשִׁ֥ים אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה יִתְקַדָּ֑שׁוּ [and also the priests who come near to the LORD shall sanctify themselves]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 19:22: Καὶ οἱ ἱερεῖς οἱ ἐγγίζοντες Κυρίῳ τῷ Θεῷ ἁγιασθήτωσαν [and let the priests who draw near to the Lord God be sanctified]. KJV 19:24: “but let not the priests and the people break through to come up unto the Lord”. KJV 19:6: “And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation.” KJV 24:5: “And he sent young men of the children of Israel, which offered burnt offerings, and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen unto the Lord.” KJV 28:1: “And take thou unto thee Aaron thy brother, and his sons with him, from among the children of Israel, that he may minister unto me in the priest's office”. KJV 13:2: “Sanctify unto me all the firstborn”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/19/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO19.htm.
reasoning: Exodus 19:22 and 19:24 treat “the priests” as a known group, distinct from the people, who already come near to the Lord. Nothing earlier in Exodus says that Israel has priests, who they are, or how they were chosen; the instruction to take Aaron and his sons for the priest’s office comes nine chapters later. At the covenant sacrifice in 24:5 the offerings are made by “young men of the children of Israel”, not by anyone called a priest.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That these priests were the firstborn sanctified at 13:2, or the young men of 24:5, or Aaron’s sons named before their appointment, are all readings; the checked passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV of Genesis and of Exodus 1–19 containing “priest” or “priests” was read. Before 19:22 the word is used of Melchizedek, of Egyptian priests, of the priest of Midian, and at 19:6 of the whole people as a promise. That is a word search of those chapters, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G is proposed: Brenton’s Greek of 19:22 has “the Lord God” where the KJV has “the Lord”, and otherwise agrees. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: What were the Urim and the Thummim, and how did they give an answer?
summary: Moses is told to put “the Urim and the Thummim” in the breastplate of judgment. Every other item of the priest’s dress is described and its making commanded. These are not: what they were, who made them, and how they gave judgment are not stated.
text: KJV Exodus 28:30: “And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron's heart, when he goeth in before the Lord: and Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the Lord continually.” Hebrew (WLC) 28:30: וְנָתַתָּ֞ אֶל־חֹ֣שֶׁן הַמִּשְׁפָּ֗ט אֶת־הָאוּרִים֙ וְאֶת־הַתֻּמִּ֔ים [and you shall put into the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 28:30: Καὶ ἐπιθήσεις ἐπὶ τὸ λογεῖον τῆς κρίσεως τὴν δήλωσιν καὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν [and you shall put upon the oracle of judgment the Manifestation and the Truth]. KJV Leviticus 8:8: “And he put the breastplate upon him: also he put in the breastplate the Urim and the Thummim.” KJV Numbers 27:21: “who shall ask counsel for him after the judgment of Urim before the Lord: at his word shall they go out, and at his word they shall come in”. KJV Deuteronomy 33:8: “Let thy Thummim and thy Urim be with thy holy one”. KJV 1 Samuel 28:6: “And when Saul enquired of the Lord, the Lord answered him not, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.” KJV Ezra 2:63: “till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim”. KJV Nehemiah 7:65: “till there stood up a priest with Urim and Thummim”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/2/28/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/EXO28.htm.
reasoning: The Urim and the Thummim are how the high priest bears “the judgment of the children of Israel”, and Numbers 27:21 makes them the means by which Joshua is to be told when to go out and come in. So they bear on how Israel is said to have received decisions from the Lord. Yet they appear with the definite article as if already known. The chapter gives the stones, the settings, the chains and the rings of the breastplate in detail, and commands that each be made; for the Urim and the Thummim it says only “put”. No passage read describes their material, their number, their maker, or what the priest did with them to get an answer.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. That they were stones, or lots that were cast, or the twelve stones of the breastplate themselves, or that the answer came by light or by the priest’s own inspiration, are all readings; the checked passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV containing “Urim” or “Thummim” was read. There are seven, and all are quoted above. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible; passages that tell of enquiring of the Lord without using either word were not searched, and the check does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The Greek names are quoted because they are translations of the two words, where the KJV keeps the Hebrew words; no G is proposed, since a translated name beside a kept one is not a difference of statement. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament.
